iut_type: QPRDv4's new mandatory IOPT (interoperability) test category, effective November 10, 2025 -- registration timing strategy to avoid the new requirement using the 180-day disclosure-date deferral
customer_question: We're targeting registration completion by November 9, 2025 -- is there any reason this specific date matters for cost or test scope, beyond our own internal schedule needs?
question_variants: What new test requirements take effect under QPRDv4, and when?
Can the public disclosure date deferral mechanism be used to avoid a new mandatory test category, not just for confidentiality purposes?
actual_issue: Beyond the customer's own internal scheduling needs, the November 9, 2025 registration deadline carried major unstated significance: Bluetooth SIG's QPRDv4 registration framework was introducing a substantial new mandatory IOPT (interoperability) test category effective November 10, 2025, covering numerous SDP Record and SDP Future Compatibility test items across nearly every profile (SR/COD, A2DP, AVRCP, DID, HFP, HID11, HSP, MAP, OPP, PAN, PBAP, SPP) -- and registrations completed before that effective date would be exempt from the entire new requirement.
plain_english_explanation: Starting November 10, 2025, QPRDv4 adds a large new mandatory IOPT (interoperability) test category spanning nearly every commonly-registered profile, with specific test items like SDP Record verification and SDP Future Compatibility checks for each profile/role combination implemented. This is a substantial new testing burden (quoted separately at ¥200,000-¥400,000 depending on what else is bundled) that did not exist for registrations completed before the effective date. Separately, Bluetooth SIG's public disclosure date mechanism was also extended around this time to allow specifying a disclosure date up to 180 days in the future (previously a shorter maximum). Combining these two facts: if the registration itself is submitted to the server by November 9, 2025 (one day before IOPT becomes mandatory), the registration is grandfathered in under the pre-IOPT rules entirely, exempting it from all RF/RF PHY and profile testing requirements that would otherwise newly apply -- even though the product's actual public disclosure/launch might happen much later, since the 180-day deferral window covers that gap. This timing strategy converts what would otherwise be a substantial new mandatory test requirement into a non-issue, purely by getting the registration submitted before the effective date cutoff.
consultant_answer: Yes, this date matters significantly beyond your own schedule: starting November 10, 2025, QPRDv4 adds a large new mandatory IOPT test category covering interoperability checks across nearly every profile you're likely registering. If your registration is completed by November 9, you're exempt from all of this -- and since the disclosure date can now be set up to 180 days out, you can register by the 9th while still controlling when the product's listing actually becomes public, without needing to rush your actual launch timeline.
decision_logic: When a customer is targeting a registration completion date in the lead-up to a known regulatory/system effective-date change (such as QPRDv4's IOPT requirement on November 10, 2025), proactively flag the cutover date's cost and scope implications rather than treating it as a purely customer-driven scheduling preference, and combine it with the public disclosure-date deferral mechanism to decouple the registration-timing deadline from the actual product launch timeline.
final_recommendation: Stay current on upcoming Bluetooth SIG registration framework effective-date changes (like QPRDv4's IOPT rollout) and proactively cross-reference any customer-stated registration deadline against such dates, since a customer's seemingly arbitrary internal deadline may actually carry major cost/scope significance they're unaware of.
risk_if_done_wrong: A customer or consultant unaware of the IOPT effective date could miss a narrow window to avoid a substantial new mandatory test category, resulting in significantly higher cost and a longer test timeline than necessary.
